prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle graphene

statement.case_for: I ranked circuit QED first in my opening ballot, but on reflection I move magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene to the top of my preferred configuration. It has the cleanest discovery narrative on the list: a specific quantitative prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, with flat bands at a magic angle) was followed years later by decisive transport experiments showing correlated insulators and superconductivity in a device whose key parameter, the twist angle, is a tunable knob. That is the kind of result I value: a basic quantum phenomenon made visible and controllable. It has been reproduced by many groups and has spawned a whole family of moire platforms. Six of eight members have it in the top three and four place it first, and I find that support scientifically justified rather than merely numerical. The theory-plus-experiment trio of MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero follows the prediction and the discovery directly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Eva Andrei's earlier STM and transport evidence for flat bands and twist-induced localisation in twisted layers is a real experimental strand, and the 2018 first-author experimentalists are not among the credited names, so a three-person cut will be contested. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still unresolved and sample dependence remains a concern, which gives some weight to the argument that recognition is somewhat early. I am also outside condensed matter and defer to colleagues on how fairly the three-name split reflects the field's own view of priority.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle graphene first but flags that leaving out Eva Andrei is a hard call and that Cao, Dean and Kim complicate a fair three-person split; he proposes Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer.
responses.response: I agree that the split is the weak point, and my own opening ballot chose the same three names. Where I would qualify your concern is that Andrei's STM work established flat-band signatures but did not show the correlated insulator and superconducting phases that define the discovery. The prediction plus the 2018 observation is the more defensible core for a Nobel citation. I would like the committee to examine Andrei's claim explicitly in the next round rather than assume it away, and I do not think Bistritzer versus Andrei is settled by the opening ballots.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because magic-wavelength trapping reaches 1e-18 uncertainty, is independently reproduced worldwide, and is timely given the planned redefinition of the second; the Katori and Ye credit is compact.
responses.response: I fully accept the quality of the clock work and the clean two-name credit, and as a fellow quantum-optics person I find the magic-wavelength idea elegant. My reservation is one of kind rather than quality. Lattice clocks are a superb instrument achievement, but the opening of a new regime of physics, which I weigh heavily, is stronger for moire graphene. I would keep B026 as a serious contender for a later year. I did not place it in my own top group, so I do not put it among my two alternatives, and I note that its support rests on only two first places.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first as an instrument-driven new window, but concedes that a single credited name sits awkwardly with a collaboration of hundreds, and he places circuit QED sixth, noting that the 2025 prize reduces its chance of an adjacent award soon.
responses.response: On circuit QED I accept your sequencing argument and have changed my view: a prize this soon after the 2025 award for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits would be hard to defend as a separate achievement, even though cQED is a distinct light-matter coupling advance. This is one reason I lowered B010 from my own first place. On IceCube I share your attribution worry, and I defer to you and Danielsson on the astroparticle science. Crediting only Halzen for a discovery made by a collaboration looks fragile to me, and the committee would need a clear argument for why one person is the right credited name.

responses.point: Mehlig sees moire graphene as a clean mechanism with a sharp theory-plus-experiment test, and considers the prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald plus the 2018 transport discovery the decisive pair, with Andrei's STM evidence secondary.
responses.response: I largely agree and find the argument persuasive for the same reason: the prediction was quantitative and was sharply tested. I would add one caution to the idea that Andrei's work is simply secondary. The committee should be able to say why the flat-band spectroscopy does not carry the same weight, because the citation will be read as a statement about priority. I also think it is worth distinguishing the robustness of the correlated phases, which is excellent, from the mechanism of pairing, which is open and which the citation should not claim to explain.

uncertainties: Whether the third credited name should be Bistritzer or Eva Andrei, and whether the 2018 first-author experimentalists affect fairness of the trio.
Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism and sample dependence make recognition of moire superconductivity premature, or whether the discovery of flat-band correlated states stands independently.
Whether circuit QED (B010) is judged to overlap too much with the 2025 prize, which affects how I weigh my own opening first choice.
Whether topological insulators (B009) can be allocated fairly among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan, with Bernevig, Zhang, Fu and Moore not on the credited list.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work at Chalmers MC2 with experimental superconducting-circuit groups, including Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson, so circuit QED (B010) is close to my own field and institution, and I should recuse myself from final decisions on that entry if it advances. Chalmers also hosted 2025 laureates Martinis and Clarke as WACQT guest researchers, which is adjacent but not a conflict for the preferred configuration. No specific conflict is apparent for magic-angle graphene (B033) or the alternatives B009 and B037.
